title: Models a Finance Ministry Can Audit

slides.title: Models a Finance Ministry Can Audit
slides.subtitle: The Climate Policy Assessment Tool, rebuilt, validated and extended: papers 4.1–4.7
slides.message: A climate-fiscal model a ministry can use must be small enough to state on a few pages, built at least twice so every step can be tested, checked against data and other models, and extended only where policy needs it.

slides.title: The problem: a model nobody can audit

stats.label: countries covered by CPAT, built by the World Bank and the IMF
words of mitigation documentation that disagreed with the model in places
legacy Excel workbook; formulas differ row by row

slides.text: Ministries set carbon prices and sequence subsidy reforms with CPAT's numbers. Until 2026 almost nobody could check them: checking one row of the workbook said little about the next.

slides.title: What CPAT computes: about eighteen equations
slides.caption: The mitigation module is a one-way chain; GDP and power prices feed back a year later (4.1).
points: Prices: supply cost, taxes, subsidies and the carbon charge.
Demand: usage and efficiency elasticities, all long-run.
Power: dispatch and investment; cost of capital 7.5–15% by income group.
$50/t cuts industrial coal by a third, road fuel by about 6%.
Road transport is described three times, and the three disagree.

slides.title: Rebuild it twice: bugs fixed, issues tracked
slides.caption: CPAT-AI register at release 1.0.2, 29 October 2026 (4.2).
points: A bug is fixed, never copied: 228 found, 24 high priority.
An issue is copied and logged: 135, plus 35 departures decided by the owner.
Excel-AI and Coded CPAT agree on every output code within 10⁻⁹.
The second build found seven bugs in the first. Built with Claude Code and GitHub Copilot.

slides.title: Validation: good for ranges, not point forecasts
slides.caption: Back-cast from 2000 with no policy, normalized RMSE of GHG (4.3).
points: Base year fits by calibration; trends fit for Australia and the US.
Baselines and price responses of the same order as IEA, Enerdata and EPM.
A $75 tax cuts G20 CO₂ 29%; elasticities move that from 7% to 39%.
Every published check predates the bug fixes.

slides.title: Elasticities: most pass, timing does not
slides.caption: CPAT defaults against published long-run estimates (4.4).
points: Seven of ten fuel-sector defaults lie in the published range.
Industrial diesel, services gasoline and services electricity are too high.
Road gasoline is double the bias-corrected mean.
The full long-run response arrives in year one; after five years only about 60% has happened.
No cross-price terms: little fuel switching outside power.

slides.title: Extend it where policy needs it
rows: Exporters' exposure to the EU border charge, product by product, and what data and a domestic price do
Turkish hot-rolled steel: €107/t in 2026, €252 at full phase-in. Egypt: verified data cut €595m to €177m a year
Investment needs priced at the cost of capital countries pay; a budget test for public money
A stylized clean asset fails above 12.6%. Kenya, Uganda, St Lucia need 4–5% of GDP in 2030
One driver layer linking CPAT, SISEPUEDE, the CBAM tool and FTT
Price response counted once; cars +64% while travel +41% in ten years (stylized)
slides.note: Country results are illustrative tool output, not official estimates.

slides.title: Rules for building policy models
slides.text: Specify the model by shared codes, build it twice, test every release, and keep every judgment with a named person.
points: Keep one register of bugs, issues, departures and upgrades, shared with the owners.
Validate as a test suite: rerun back-casts and comparisons at every release, with a measure of fit.
Extend only where a ministry asks, and count each price response once.
